name: Sara Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Out with the dogs at first light, Bess and Moss, checking the ewes on the hill. We run about six hundred ewes on the high ground above Craigside, with a few fields of hay and turnips down by the house for winter. My husband Yusuf works for the council roads team and helps at gathering and lambing. I love the hill on a clear morning when you can see three valleys, and I hate lambing in sleet, out at two in the morning with a torch in my teeth.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do the dogs and the hill shape your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Without the dogs, I couldn't do it, simple as that. A good dog does the work of three people on that slope. Bess is nine now and slowing down, and I'm training Moss, who's young and keen and doesn't listen yet, a bit like my son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, nothing more. I've used it a couple of times to check a dose for a sick ewe when the vet was out, and it was right, though I checked with the vet after. I'd say that at the mart, the livestock market, if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't touch the hill. Sheep don't care. What matters is the lamb price at the mart in autumn and whether the government keeps the hill farm payments going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd spend about three thousand on new gates for the in-bye fields, those are the fields down by the house, which need doing anyway. I'd use the chat program now and then for the paperwork, once Yusuf's sister showed me the good way to ask it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You checked its answer with the vet. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a wrong dose kills a ewe, and a ewe is a hundred and fifty lambs over her life, give or take. I trust it like I'd trust a neighbour's advice: probably right, but I'd still ring the vet. That's just sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do those hill payments matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're the difference between a profit and a loss most years. I'm not a fan of handouts, but this isn't one: we keep the hills grazed, the walls standing and the paths open. If they went, half the farms up here would go.

S0.say: It's a useful tool, nothing more. I've used it to check a dose for a sick ewe when the vet was out, and it was right.
S0.think: It doesn't touch the hill, because sheep don't care. What matters is the autumn lamb price at the mart and whether the hill farm payments continue.
S0.do: Spends about three thousand on new gates for the fields by the house, as planned. Uses the chat program now and then for paperwork, once a relative shows her how to ask it well.
S0.quote: I'm not a fan of handouts, but this isn't one: we keep the hills grazed, the walls standing and the paths open.
S0.fieldNote: She uses AI carefully and checks its answers with the vet, treating it like a neighbour's advice. She drew a firm line between handouts and hill farm payments, which she sees as earned. Her dogs are central to how she describes her work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sad to see beginners struggle, but young people up here have always had to go away for work. What they need is apprenticeships and a reason to come back. I'd say it at church and at the young farmers' club dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, slow is fine for me. But my son Adam is seventeen and wants to be a mechanic in town, and our daughter Maryam wants to go to college. If companies hire fewer beginners, they'll both have to go further, and the hill gets emptier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the garage in town to take Adam on Saturdays, so he's in the door. I'd keep the flock the same. Maybe try the electronic ear-tag reader the mart uses, once the other hill farmers have, because it saves writing every number by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, quietly. It's the emptiness I worry about, not the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by the hill getting emptier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I was a girl there were seven families farming this valley. Now there are three. The school closed in 2015, the chapel has eight people on a good Sunday. Every young person who leaves for good is another light out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Adam ever come back to farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if there's a living. He's good with the quad and the dogs like him. I'd rather he went away, learned a trade, and came back with money in his pocket than stayed and scraped.

S1.say: It's sad to see beginners struggle, but young people up here have always gone away for work. They need apprenticeships and a reason to come back.
S1.think: Slow change is fine for me, but my son and daughter would have to go further for their first jobs. Every family that leaves makes the hill emptier.
S1.do: Asks the garage in town to take Adam on Saturdays so he gets a foot in the door. Keeps the flock the same and tries the mart's electronic ear-tag reader once other hill farmers have.
S1.feel: Quietly uneasy about the emptiness, not the money.
S1.quote: Every young person who leaves for good is another light out.
S1.fieldNote: Her real worry is the valley emptying: seven farming families down to three, the school and chapel shrinking. She'd rather her son left, learned a trade and came back with money. Her technology choices follow other hill farmers, one step behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should be helped to find new work, not paid to sit at home. The politicians arguing gets nobody anywhere. I'd say that online, and I'd say it plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, Yusuf's job worries me. He's on the council roads team, outdoors mostly, but there's talk of the council cutting office staff, and when councils cut, they cut everywhere. His wage covers the mortgage and the kids' things, the sheep cover the rest, just about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Yusuf and work out what we'd do on the sheep alone if his wage went. I'd look at selling more lambs direct to butchers, maybe forty, for a better price than the mart. And I'd keep the four months of savings, and maybe stop the gates job until we know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, but the knot's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if Yusuf lost his job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday we take at the coast every August, a week in a caravan. Then the kids' extras. The dogs' food and the vet bill I'd not touch, they're the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said help people find work, not pay them. What if Yusuf needed help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd want it to be help finding him another job, not a cheque. He'd hate a cheque, he'd feel useless. A man like him needs to be out working, or he goes quiet and sits in the shed.

S2.say: People should be helped to find new work, not paid to sit at home. The politicians arguing gets nobody anywhere.
S2.think: My husband's council job worries me, because when councils cut, they cut everywhere. His wage covers the mortgage, and the sheep cover the rest, just about.
S2.do: Works out with Yusuf how they'd live on the sheep alone and starts selling about forty lambs direct to butchers. Keeps the four months' savings and pauses the gates job.
S2.feel: Anxious, not panicked, but with a knot of worry.
S2.quote: He'd hate a cheque, he'd feel useless. A man like him needs to be out working, or he goes quiet and sits in the shed.
S2.fieldNote: Her public line against paying people to sit at home was consistent even when I asked about her own husband. She'd want him helped into work, not given money, and she described what idleness would do to him. The dogs and vet bill are the last things she'd cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people who earn it should keep it, but everyone should pay their share, and the country should look after its own. I'd want the gains to go into the countryside too, not just the cities. I'd say that at the mart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, sheep are physical, they're safe. But booming house prices bring people from the city up here buying holiday homes, and then local young families can't afford to live in the valley. I've seen it with the cottage at the bottom of the lane, sold for twice what anyone local could pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the farm steady and fix our mortgage. I'd talk to the parish council about keeping a few houses for local families, which is something I'd actually stand up for. And I'd sell more lambs direct, because city people with money like to know where their meat comes from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit sad. The hill is safe but the valley might not be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened to the cottage at the bottom of the lane?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Mrs Reid lived there for fifty years. When she died, a couple from the city bought it, and they come up four weekends a year. The lights are off the rest of the time, and nobody's children are playing in that garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd want rules on who buys houses. Is that at odds with free markets?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. I believe in people earning and keeping, but a village isn't just a market, it's families and a church and a school. Some things you protect, even if it costs.

S3.say: People who earn it should keep it, but everyone should pay their share and the country should look after its own. The gains should reach the countryside, not just the cities.
S3.think: Sheep are physical work and safe. But booming house prices bring city buyers for holiday homes, and local young families can't afford to stay in the valley.
S3.do: Keeps the farm steady and fixes the mortgage. Asks the parish council to keep some houses for local families, and sells more lambs direct to well-off city buyers.
S3.feel: Uneasy and a little sad: the hill is safe but the valley may not be.
S3.quote: The lights are off the rest of the time, and nobody's children are playing in that garden.
S3.fieldNote: She feels safe in her own work but sees the boom hollowing out the valley through holiday homes. When I raised the tension with her free-market views, she admitted it and argued a village is more than a market. The story of Mrs Reid's cottage carried the whole scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on lowland farms are one thing, but they'll struggle on a hill. I'd also say the government shouldn't pay for big companies to put them in. People need work, that's what keeps a community together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm less worried than the lowland farmers. A robot on a forty-degree slope in sleet, I'd like to see it. But drones gathering sheep, maybe, and if the lowland farms get much cheaper, the lamb price drops, and that hurts us anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see, but I'd watch closely. I'd go to the hill farming show and look at the drones, and if the neighbour tried one for gathering, I might try it next year. I'd also push harder on selling lambs as hill-reared, with a story, because that's what a robot farm can't copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, not alarmed. I worry for the lowland people more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a drone replace Bess and Moss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in my lifetime. A drone can find sheep, but it can't hold them against a wall in the wind or sense a ewe's about to break. Maybe it saves me a walk up to the top on a foggy day, and I'd take that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the lowland people you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Hassan has a dairy farm in the valley floor, and his workers, two lads from the village. If robots come there, those lads have nowhere to go. I'd want them to have work, not a cheque, and I'd ask around for them.

S4.say: Robots on lowland farms are one thing, but they'll struggle on a hill. The government shouldn't pay big companies to put them in, because work keeps a community together.
S4.think: I'm less worried than lowland farmers, because I'd like to see a robot on a forty-degree slope in sleet. But if lowland farms get cheaper, the lamb price drops and that hurts us anyway.
S4.do: Goes to the hill farming show to look at gathering drones and tries one a year after a neighbour does. Pushes harder on selling lambs as hill-reared, with a story a robot farm can't copy.
S4.feel: Anxious rather than alarmed, and more worried for lowland workers than for herself.
S4.quote: A drone can find sheep, but it can't hold them against a wall in the wind or sense a ewe's about to break.
S4.fieldNote: Unlike most farmers here, she reacts less sharply to robots because steep hill land protects her. She still saw the price risk clearly. Her worry turned outward to her cousin's farm workers, and she'd want them helped into work, not paid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Strange to say, the fast one, the third one, with house prices booming. Not for the sheep but for the valley, the holiday homes and the young families going. What would help is rules that keep some houses for local people, and apprenticeships so the young ones have a reason to stay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the dogs. Nobody ever asks about the dogs, and they're half the farm. If you write about hill farming and don't mention a dog, you've not been on a hill.

headlineQuote: A robot on a forty-degree slope in sleet, I'd like to see it.
portrait: Sara is a 43-year-old hill sheep farmer with about six hundred ewes above Craigside, working with her dogs Bess and Moss while her husband Yusuf works on the council roads team. She holds traditional views on faith, family and work, and uses AI now and then but checks it with the vet. Her worries run less to her own job than to her valley emptying, from young people leaving to city buyers turning cottages into holiday homes. Steep hill land makes her calmer than most about robots, and the house-price boom worries her more than the machines.
biggestWorry: The fast scenario with booming house prices, because holiday homes and departing young families could empty her valley.
whatWouldHelp: Rules keeping some houses for local people, and apprenticeships that give young people a reason to stay.
